1	---
2	name: extract-from-conversations
3	description: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
4	---
5	
6	# Extract lessons from a conversation
7	
8	The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
9	taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
10	dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
11	what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.
12	
13	The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
14	surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
15	re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.
16	
17	## The goal
18	
19	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
20	waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
21	cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
22	a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.
23	
24	## Where the conversation comes from
25	
26	- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
27	  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
28	  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
29	  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
30	- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
31	  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.
32	
33	**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
34	when a session is done enough to mine.
35	
36	## What to look for — the friction signals
37	
38	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
39	necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
40	
41	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
42	
43	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
44	building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
45	answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
46	
47	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
48	user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
49	a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
50	the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
51	correctly **without the round-trip**.
52	
53	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
54	
55	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
56	that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
57	something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
58	convention and had it corrected in review.
59	
60	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
61	so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
62	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
63	first, not after a detour.
64	
65	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
66	
67	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
68	padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
69	hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.
70	
71	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
72	and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
73	(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
74	only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
75	was already optimal.
76	
77	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
78	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
79	the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
80	a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
81	loss of quality.
82	
83	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
84	
85	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
86	checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
87	fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
88	fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
89	relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
90	recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
91	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.
92	
93	## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch
94	
95	Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:
96	
97	- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
98	- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
99	  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
100	  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
101	  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.
102	
103	The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
104	stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
105	every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
106	breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.
107	
108	## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it
109	
110	For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
111	(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
112	nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):
113	
114	- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
115	- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
116	  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.
117	
118	**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
119	beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
120	**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
121	deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
122	silence it replaced.
123

## Report — issue-332 conversation log

**No durable TLDR-repo lesson found.** This session's task itself is Claudinite meta-plumbing (`claudinite-growth/growth-discover-packs`, a weekly reflection scanning the repo for pack-worthy knowledge), which the task brief explicitly excludes: lessons about "the engine's own loading mechanics" are filed upstream, not as a TLDR project rule.

**The one real friction signal observed doesn't qualify, on the same exclusion.** The session hit a ~4-minute diagnostic detour (05:20:11–05:24:15Z) rediscovering that `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/converge-item.mjs` can't authenticate directly against the GitHub REST API in this sandboxed/proxied session (`GITHUB_REPOSITORY` unset → direct `curl` to `api.github.com` returns `403` → `gh.mjs` with `GITHUB_TOKEN` returns `401 Bad credentials` → git-config extraheader probe blocked by the auto-mode classifier), before falling back to replicating the script's five convergence side-effects by hand via `mcp__github__*` tools. The session's own closing comment notes this is "the same limitation #335 hit earlier in this batch" — i.e., this is a recurring, already-known failure mode of `converge-item.mjs` itself under Claude Code Web's proxy, not anything about TLDR's code or conventions. Its fix (auto-detect the environment and fall back to MCP, or document the limitation) belongs in the Claudinite engine, not `.claudinite/local/packs/tldr/RULES.md`.

**No other friction found.** No misunderstandings (no user turns at all — this is an unattended scheduler-fired session with an empty routine-fire payload as its only "user" input). No Edit/Write tool calls occurred anywhere in the log — the session was pure read-only investigation. The pack survey itself (dev/procedures, dev/docs, server/, extension/, shared/, dev/requirements/) concluded honestly that no repo segment held reusable knowledge both ungrounded elsewhere and distinct enough for a new local pack — a legitimate "nothing found" outcome per the task's own contract, not a missed opportunity.

**Session summary (provenance):** An unattended `growth-discover-packs` run against issue #332 surveyed the TLDR repo's structure (extension, server, shared modules, dev/requirements) against the existing canon pack shelf and the local `tldr` pack, concluded no new local pack was warranted, then closed #332 with that finding — hand-replicating `converge-item.mjs`'s label/comment/close sequence via MCP tools after the script's direct GitHub REST auth failed in this session's environment.

Session id: `0977b66d-0023-5c3c-a26f-bc9a7bccf461`. Issue: `missingbulb/TLDR#332`.

## Report: conversation-logs / issue-114 (session 2465826e-f016-5b6f-bf25-ab62700d65e9)

**No durable lesson found** that clears the bar for `.claudinite/local/packs/tldr/RULES.md`.

### Why

This log is the Claudinite **executor + growth-extract task itself** (dispatch issue #114, `[claudinite-task] grow_with_claudinite/growth-extract d2026-07-26`) — exactly the meta-plumbing category the instructions say to exclude unless the friction is about working in the TLDR repo specifically. Its one substantive product — a new local pack lesson titled "the three version records, and the two the pipeline actually bumps" (committed in PR #120, merged at `e256fa4`) — has since been **superseded**: the current `.claudinite/local/packs/tldr/RULES.md` carries a materially different, later-dated version of that same topic ("This repo's copy of the bump-version workflow is deliberately not the canon stub," referencing the 2026-08-21 release-model overhaul and open issue #245). So there's nothing left to extract on that front; it already landed and was overwritten by subsequent real work.

Friction points found, each weighed and rejected:

- **Suboptimal action**: a `Bash cat >` heredoc created `validate.mjs`, then a `node` run failed (`ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`), then the agent tried the `Write` tool on the same path and got `"File has not been read yet. Read it first before writing to it."` (turns ~52–60, ~15s). This is the same mechanic already generalized in `CLAUDE.md`'s harness-tool-contracts section for `Edit` ("must have been read with the read tool; cat/grep/sed don't count") — extending it to `Write` is a marginal, quickly self-corrected hiccup, not a new durable rule.
- **Backtrack**: the executor opened a throwaway housekeeping PR (#119, a `.gitignore` fix for `.claude/worktrees/`) on its own designated scratch branch, later had to `git reset --hard origin/main` and close it because it collided with the `feature-requirements-first` check on the branch meant for the growth-extract PR. A `git push --force-with-lease` was blocked by "the Claude Code auto mode classifier," worked around by relying on the fact the local Stop-hook check reads local history only. This is entirely about the **executor's own scratch-branch mechanics**, not TLDR-repo convention — belongs upstream if anywhere, not this pack.
- **Minor/borderline**: `enable_pr_auto_merge` failed outright — `"Auto-merge is not enabled for this repository."` — a real, checkable TLDR repo-settings fact, but it's a single wasted call immediately recovered via manual merge, not a "cost more than it should have" pattern, and repo settings can change under it. Not worth a rule.
- No long-wall-time or serialization waste found; the one ~19-minute gap (21:58→22:17) was the session correctly idling for the human's external "lgtm 120" trigger, not agent-caused.

### Session summary (provenance)

Session `2465826e-f016-5b6f-bf25-ab62700d65e9`, issue **#114** — the Claudinite executor picked up the `grow_with_claudinite/growth-extract` daily task, validated the dispatch, launched a background subagent that reviewed four recent commits/three issue threads, found one lesson (the chrome-extension version-sync gotcha), authored the repo's first local pack, opened PR #120, and the parent session merged it on the owner's "lgtm". A stray throwaway PR (#119) was opened and cleanly closed along the way.

# TLDR — repo rules

## A green release run is not evidence the store publish works

The daily auto-release short-circuits at `daily / check` when nothing under the release config's
`ship_paths` changed since the last release tag, so `Release to Chrome Store` concludes **success**
with the `daily / publish` job skipped entirely. Since the scheduler cutover (#107) the daily leg
runs only when the Claudinite scheduler dispatches this workflow in `mode: daily`, so a real publish
is rarer still — most green runs never touched the store.

When triaging a publish-leg failure, read the **`daily / publish` job**, not the run conclusion. The
open example is #93/#94 (run 29229001858): three separate triage passes (07-16, 07-18, 07-26) each
re-derived that no later run had re-executed the step, and each re-nominated whichever repo-side bug
happened to be open at the time as the "suspected root cause, unconfirmed". Two things settle it and
are worth not re-deriving a fourth time:

- **`ITEM_NOT_UPDATABLE` is Chrome Web Store-side state** — a prior submission still pending review
  or ready to publish — so **nothing in `main` can be "the fix"**, and no repo-side defect that
  happened to be open at the time (a stale secret, a half-landed config) should be credited with it.
- **The only closing evidence is a run that actually reaches `daily / publish` and goes green**, or
  the Chrome Developer Dashboard showing the item out of pending/review. Absent that, the issue stays
  open — resolving the co-occurring repo bug is not the same as verifying the publish path.

## This repo's copy of the bump-version workflow is deliberately not the canon stub

The canon line for a vendored file — *never hand-edit these copies, the template is canon* —
does **not** hold for whichever workflow carries the repo's one local delta: a step that aligns
the repo-root `package.json` to a version the pipeline just bumped, load-bearing since the
release config only bumps `manifest_path` and `package_json_path`. `chrome-release-vendoring`'s
materialize is an unconditional verbatim overwrite with no per-repo exemption seam, so the step

content.content:
1	// The machine-readable records a task's execution leaves in an Actions log
2	// (skill-usage-metrics DESIGN §4.2), and the parsers that read them back.
3	//
4	// TWO FAMILIES, ONE OF THEM HISTORICAL. `claudinite-task-run` was the SLOT
5	// scheduler's own line, one per due task per run; the slot scheduler is retired
6	// (#974) and nothing writes that line any more. The parser stays, and only the
7	// parser: Actions logs from before the retirement are still inside their retention
8	// window, and the usage fold still counts them. Nothing new should be taught this
9	// shape — `claudinite-task-exec` below is the live record.
10	//
11	// The counts these produce are exact within the Actions log retention window, and
12	// that is worth stating next to the capture-derived counts they land beside.
13	
14	// The five things a slot scheduler run could do with a due task. One name per
15	// outcome, used verbatim as the counter key in the aggregate, so there is no
16	// mapping table between "what the run said" and "what the fold counted" to drift.
17	export const TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES = Object.freeze([
18	  // A dispatch issue was filed: an agent session ran this task.
19	  'agent',
20	  // The task ran with NO agent — an `agent_model: none` task (code-work is the
21	  // whole task), or an agentful one whose code-work requested no agent phase.
22	  // Kebab, not the declaration field's `code_work`: this word is a WIRE token,
23	  // constrained to the line format's `[a-z-]+` charset.
24	  'code-work',
25	  // Due, but its precondition said there was nothing to do.
26	  'skipped',
27	  // Its code-work failed; the run converged the task to a needs-human issue.
28	  'failed',
29	  // Due and past its precondition, but no NEW agent run started: this slot was
30	  // already dispatched (exactly-once), an earlier dispatch is still open
31	  // (at-most-one-open), or another task claimed the run exclusively. Work that
32	  // was wanted and did not happen this run.
33	  'deferred',
34	]);
35	
36	// An empty per-task counter row — every outcome present, zeros included, so a row's
37	// shape never depends on which outcomes a task happened to hit.
38	export const emptyTaskRun = () => Object.fromEntries(TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES.map((o) => [o, 0]));
39	
40	// The line format. `v1` is the shape's version: a reader that meets a `v2` line
41	// knows it is looking at something it was not written for, instead of silently
42	// half-parsing it.
43	export const TASK_RUN_TAG = 'claudinite-task-run';
44	const VERSION = 'v1';
45	
46	// Actions stamps every log line with its own timestamp before the command's output,
47	// so the parse tolerates that prefix — without it, a fetched log reads as having
48	// printed nothing at all.
49	const LINE_RE = new RegExp(
50	  String.raw`^(?:\S+\s+)?${TASK_RUN_TAG} ${VERSION} (\S+)/(\S+) \[(\S+)\] ([a-z-]+)\s*$`,
51	);
52	
53	// One line → `{ pack, task, slotId, outcome }`, or null for anything that is not a
54	// record of this version. Deliberately strict: an unknown outcome word is NOT a
55	// record, because counting it would mint a counter key nothing ever reads.
56	// The code phase has been renamed twice, and job logs outlive both renames:
57	// `preprocess` (pre-2026-08-06) and `prework` (pre-2026-08-18) are the earlier
58	// words for what is now `code-work`. Runs logged under either still parse, each
59	// normalized straight to the canonical word.
60	// Exported because the outcome words are also the usage aggregate's counter KEYS,
61	// and that file holds rows written under the older words. Its decode renames them
62	// by this same map, so a rename never silently drops a historical count.
63	export const LEGACY_TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES = Object.freeze({ preprocess: 'code-work', prework: 'code-work' });
64	
65	export function parseTaskRun(line) {
66	  const m = LINE_RE.exec(line);
67	  if (!m) return null;
68	  const [, pack, task, slotId, word] = m;
69	  const outcome = LEGACY_TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES[word] ?? word;
70	  if (!TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES.includes(outcome)) return null;
71	  return { pack, task, slotId, outcome };
72	}
73	
74	// Every record in one job log. The log is the whole job's output — this picks its
75	// own lines out of it and ignores everything else.
76	export function parseTaskRuns(text) {
77	  const out = [];
78	  for (const line of String(text ?? '').split('\n')) {
79	    const rec = parseTaskRun(line);
80	    if (rec) out.push(rec);
81	  }
82	  return out;
83	}
84	
85	// --- executor-side execution records ------------------------------------------
86	// The historical records above say what the retired slot scheduler DID with a due
87	// task; these record what an EXECUTOR SESSION did with the work it ran. Printed by executor-side code
88	// (resolve-dispatch on a terminal verdict, record-exec.mjs at convergence), they
89	// land in the session transcript, ride to the conversation-logs branch with the
90	// executor's capture step, and the usage fold counts them deterministically —
91	// the "task statuses out of the conversation logs" half of the census (owner,
92	// 2026-08-06). Same single-home rule: renderer and parser sit here together.
93	
94	export const TASK_EXEC_STATUSES = Object.freeze([
95	  // The dispatch ran to completion within its ceiling; the issue was closed.
96	  'success',
97	  // The run failed (task failure or ceiling violation); converged to needs-human.
98	  'failed',
99	  // The dispatch named a task the repo no longer carries (file gone, pack
100	  // undeclared) — the executor closed the issue as obsolete. Not a failure.
101	  'task-gone',
102	  // The dispatch was malformed (bad path shape, unparseable declaration) and was
103	  // converged to needs-human without running.
104	  'invalid',
105	]);
106	
107	export const TASK_EXEC_TAG = 'claudinite-task-exec';
108	
109	// The bracketed field is the OCCURRENCE'S IDENTITY, which is a different thing under
110	// each dispatch mechanism: a slot id (`d2026-08-06`) where slots decide what runs, and
111	// the work item's issue number (`#867`) where the queue does. `slotId` keeps its name
112	// for the fielded records that already carry one; what it must never become is a
113	// constant, since it is the only join from a record back to the work it describes.
114	export const renderTaskExec = ({ pack, task, slotId, status }) =>
115	  `${TASK_EXEC_TAG} ${VERSION} ${pack}/${task} [${slotId ?? 'unknown'}] ${status}`;
116	
117	const EXEC_LINE_RE = new RegExp(
118	  String.raw`(?:^|\s)${TASK_EXEC_TAG} ${VERSION} (\S+)/(\S+) \[(\S+)\] ([a-z-]+)\s*$`,
119	);
120	
121	export function parseTaskExec(line) {
122	  const m = EXEC_LINE_RE.exec(line);
123	  if (!m) return null;
124	  const [, pack, task, slotId, status] = m;
125	  if (!TASK_EXEC_STATUSES.includes(status)) return null;
126	  return { pack, task, slotId, status };
127	}
128

1	// APPLYING a status transition — the write half of the vocabulary whose read half
2	// is `work-item.mjs`'s decode (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §4, the migration of #1119).
3	//
4	// One rule, and it is why this is not a plain `swapLabel`: the item may wear ANY
5	// engine version's spelling of the status it is leaving. A member's items outlive
6	// its converges, so an item filed as `task:ready` is picked up by an engine that
7	// writes `task:status:waiting-for-executor`, and a swap that named one spelling
8	// would leave the other standing — an item wearing two live statuses, which is the
9	// torn state the janitor exists to repair.
10	//
11	// Writes stay granular (add and remove named labels, never a set-write): with
12	// several executors and a scheduler run moving labels at once, a set-write from a
13	// stale snapshot clobbers a concurrent transition (DESIGN §4).
14	// The removes are UNCONDITIONAL — every spelling of the status being left, not
15	// only the ones the caller's snapshot shows. A caller holds the labels it read
16	// before its own earlier transitions, so filtering on that snapshot would skip
17	// exactly the label this engine just wrote; removing a label an issue does not
18	// carry 404s, which is the end state asked for and therefore success.
19	import { spellingsOf } from './work-item.mjs';
20	
21	// Move `item` out of `fromStatus` (canonical — every spelling of it goes) and into
22	// the label `to`, which is whatever spelling this engine writes.
23	export async function swapStatus(api, gh, repo, item, fromStatus, to) {
24	  await clearStatus(api, gh, repo, item, fromStatus);
25	  return api.addLabel(gh, repo, item.number, to);
26	}
27	
28	// Leave a status without entering another — the close path, where the terminal
29	// label is applied separately.
30	export async function clearStatus(api, gh, repo, item, status) {
31	  for (const label of spellingsOf(status)) {
32	    await api.removeLabel(gh, repo, item.number, label);
33	  }
34	}
